wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about their summer—one false. They mingle, share, and guess the lie. They say, 'I learned French,' 'I visited the Sahara,' 'I ate couscous every day.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students interview peers to find who 'watched an English movie,' 'traveled to another city,' or 'started a new hobby.' They ask, 'Did you...?' and tally responses.

Speed Introductions: In pairs, students introduce themselves with name, job, and one English goal. They rotate every 30 seconds, saying, 'My name is ___, I'm a ___, and I want to learn English for ___.'
pres: Display flashcards with opinion phrases ('I think,' 'In my opinion,' 'From my perspective'). Model sentences: 'I think learning English is important for work.' 'In my opinion, practice is key.' Check understanding by asking, 'What phrase means you have a personal view?'
presAlt: Realia with local context: Show a photo of the American Space Oujda. Ask, 'What do you think about this space?' Elicit opinions, then model phrases.
Short dialogue: Read a dialogue between two learners discussing their goals. Highlight opinion phrases and ask students to underline them.
prac: Opinion Circles: Students sit in groups of 3. Each group gets a topic (e.g., 'Learning English online vs. in class'). They take turns sharing opinions using target phrases. I monitor and prompt, 'Say what you think.'
pracAlt: Matching game: Match opinion phrases to sentence starters ('I believe...', 'It seems to me...'). Students practice in pairs, completing sentences.
Role-play cards: Students draw cards with topics (e.g., 'Best way to learn vocabulary') and role-play a conversation using opinion language.
ls: PET-style listening: Play a short audio of two people discussing their learning goals. Students listen and write down two opinion phrases they hear. They compare in pairs, saying, 'I heard 'In my opinion, speaking is hard.''
re: Quick Poll: After the break, I ask, 'Who thinks English is useful for travel?' Students stand up if yes, sit if no. They shout 'I agree!' or 'I disagree!'
prod: Diagnostic Discussion Groups: Students form groups of 4. Each group discusses, 'What are your personal goals for English this year?' They use opinion phrases and note one goal per person. They report back, 'Fatima thinks she wants to improve her writing.'
rw: PET Orientation: Students read a short text about the PET exam (from the PET folder). They map the sections (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking) and discuss, 'Which part do you think is hardest?' They write one sentence about their goal, e.g., 'I want to pass the PET speaking test.'
st: Closing song: Play a short, upbeat English song (e.g., 'Happy' by Pharrell Williams). Students wave and sing along. End with: 'Today we practiced opinions and set goals. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 9 opinion phrases in a grid. I call out phrases; they cross them off. First to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
I read a statement (e.g., 'English is easy'). Students stand if they agree, sit if not. They must say why using 'I think...'
One student starts a sentence (e.g., 'I think coffee is delicious'). The next adds, 'In my opinion, it's better than tea.'
Students write goals on cards. Mix and redistribute. They read a card and say, 'I think [name] wants to...'
Label corners with 'Strongly Agree,' 'Agree,' 'Disagree,' 'Strongly Disagree.' I read statements; students move to corners and justify.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about their best learning experience using opinion phrases.
Support weaker learners: Use sentence starters (e.g., 'I think... because...') to scaffold their goal-setting.
hw: Write an 8-sentence paragraph about your English goals. Use 'I think' and 'In my opinion.'
Record a 1-minute voice note explaining why you want to learn English. Send it to the teacher.
Read a short article about learning English (provided) and write 3 opinions using today's phrases.
tip: Leverage the American Space Oujda context by connecting goals to real-world opportunities, like accessing English resources or participating in U.S.-Morocco exchange programs. This increases motivation.
